source.title: Rodent model of infant attachment learning and stress.

confidence_rationale: Review of Sullivan-lab infant rat work: during postnatal days 1-9 pups readily learn odor preferences while fear/aversion learning is attenuated, so they learn to approach the caregiver regardless of care quality; after ~PN10 rising corticosterone enables amygdala-dependent fear learning. That is strong mechanistic support for an innate, approach-biased coupling phase preceding a phase with full threat learning. But the transition is reversible: maternal presence restores preference learning and suppresses fear learning in PN10-15 pups, so the phase boundary is gated by the caregiver's presence, not a one-way switch.
failure_signatures: Rodent olfactory attachment learning maps only loosely onto human attachment or an artificial agent.
Approach learning that persists regardless of care quality (including to an abusive caregiver) shows phase 1 coupling is not selective for a 'competent' environment, contrary to the claim's framing.

mapping.source_claim_statement: Infant rats show a sensitive period (PN1-9) of enhanced odor-preference and attenuated fear learning, overlapping the stress-hyporesponsive period; after PN10 corticosterone permits amygdala-dependent fear learning; maternal presence reinstates preference learning and suppresses fear in PN10-15 pups via suppression of corticosterone and amygdala activity.
mapping.ree_translation: Mechanistic analogue of ARC-122 phase (1) -> (2): an early learning regime biased toward coupling to the caregiver, followed by a transition that opens threat learning. The caregiver acts as a social buffer that can re-open the earlier regime.
mapping.mapping_caveat: The window is caregiver-gated and reversible, which supports graded/overlapping windows rather than strict sequencing; and phase-1 coupling occurs even to a poor caregiver, so 'competent environment' is not a precondition of the mechanism.
mapping.source_context: Review of Sullivan-lab rodent developmental neurobiology (olfactory bulb, locus coeruleus norepinephrine, corticosterone, amygdala).

confidence_components.notes: Named Sullivan anchor verified; companion review Sullivan & Holman 2010 (PMID 19931556) covers the same transitions.
